title: SYSK Selects: How Wine Fraud Works
summary: SYSK Selects episode, a rerun of the October 2015 episode "How Wine Fraud Works," introduced by Chuck. The hosts discuss wine counterfeiting: the history of wine fraud (including ancient Rome and lead sweetening), the Tesco Louis Roederer knockoff, the debate over how widespread fraud is, and whether wine tasters can tell wines apart. They profile Bill Koch, who bought fake vintage wine, and counterfeiter Rudy Kurniawan, who sold fakes and was convicted and sentenced to ten years. They also cover Hardy Rodenstock and the Thomas Jefferson bottles (the "TH" vs "T.J." engraving, cesium-137 dating, and the Monticello doubts), methods of faking wine (refilling real bottles or relabeling cheaper vintages), anti-fraud measures such as RFID tags, tamper-evident capsules and DNA-marked labels, empty-bottle sales on eBay, and the restaurant practice of smashing empty vintage bottles. The episode ends with listener Facebook and Twitter questions on research methods, favorite beers and cities, and other light topics.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Selects episode, a pick from October 2015 on wine fraud. The hosts open with small talk about coffee smell and then turn to whether people really know the wine they drink.

segments.title: Wine fraud scope and history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Tesco case in Britain where a counterfeit Louis Roederer was sold at a discount. They note the debate over how widespread wine fraud is and that it has existed since ancient Rome, when lead was added to sweeten wine.

segments.title: Can people really tell wine apart?
segments.summary: The hosts discuss blind tastings where wines were swapped, the snobbery debate, and how collectors judge old wine against past experience, which counterfeiters can exploit. They also note that many collectors buy old bottles to display them rather than drink them.

segments.title: Bill Koch and his collection
segments.summary: Bill Koch, a billionaire who left the family business and collects rare items such as guns and art, is described as the most famous victim of wine fraud. He sued many sellers. A sample of three thousand of his bottles yielded about 130 fakes, and he reportedly spent close to five million dollars on fake wine over about 25 years.

segments.title: Rudy Kurniawan's counterfeiting
segments.summary: Rudy Kurniawan is described as one of the most notorious wine counterfeiters. He was sentenced to ten years in prison, and the hosts describe how he built a reputation through lavish dinners, bought up old vintages, and was caught after a mistake about a Ponsot Clos Saint-Denis. The hosts also mention his ongoing appeal.

segments.title: Ways to fake wine
segments.summary: The hosts explain two methods: faking the wine inside a real bottle, or putting real wine in a fake bottle. They describe using older vintages that are harder to date and relabeling vintage bottles to raise their value.

segments.title: Hardy Rodenstock and the Jefferson bottles
segments.summary: Hardy Rodenstock, a self-described wine collector, is said to have sold Thomas Jefferson bottles to billionaires. The bottles were engraved with a 'Th' initial and a 'J' with a misplaced punctuation mark. Historians doubted the engraving and the claim. Testing with cesium-137 was one line of inquiry. The hosts stress the case was resolved civilly, not in court, and Rodenstock denies the allegations.

segments.title: Anti-counterfeiting measures and eBay
segments.summary: The hosts describe modern anti-fraud tools: RFID tags, QR codes, tamper-evident neck capsules, and DNA markers in label ink. They also discuss empty vintage bottles sold on eBay and restaurants that smash empty bottles to prevent refilling. They also mention a claim that counterfeits of a rare Fleur wine outnumbered the bottles produced.

segments.title: Show close-out: wine fraud search tip
segments.summary: Chuck points listeners to the How Stuff Works site to search for more on wine fraud.

segments.title: Facebook and Twitter listener questions
segments.summary: The hosts answer listener questions about research sources and peer-reviewed journals, favorite beers and homebrewing, favorite cities, pop tart flavors, and rewarding aspects of the show.

segments.title: Outro and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give ways to get in touch: Facebook, Twitter, email, and the website.
